title: The staff and the termite
hookLine: Sulayman dies leaning on his staff, and only a termite eating it reveals his death to the jinn (34:14)

lines: A KING LEANS ON HIS STAFF.
HE HAD BEEN DEAD THE WHOLE TIME.
cards: A king stands leaning on his staff, watching his workers. They are jinn, beings of smokeless fire, building for him: high halls, statues, basins like wells. They work hard, because he's watching.
Time passes. He doesn't move. They keep working.
Then something tiny, something none of them noticed, finishes its own quiet job inside the wood. The staff gives way. The king falls.
He had been dead the whole time. This is Sulayman, son of Dawud, and one of the Qur'an's quietest death scenes.

teach.h: A CREATURE OF THE EARTH, EATING THE STAFF.
teach.b: Surah Saba', verse fourteen. Pickthall: "nothing showed his death to them save a creeping creature of the earth which gnawed away his staff." The Arabic is dabbat al-ard, a creature of the earth.
The verse doesn't name the species. Commentators understand a woodworm or termite, which is where today's title comes from. How long Sulayman stood there, the Qur'an doesn't say.

teach.h: HOW LONG? THE TEXT IS SILENT.
teach.b: Some commentators guess a long while; the text is silent.

teach.h: THE JINN DIDN'T KNOW THE UNSEEN.
teach.b: Then the point: when he fell, the jinn saw clearly that if they had known the unseen, they wouldn't have kept on in humiliating toil. Here's why that stings.

Commentators explain that jinn were thought to know hidden things, and fortune-tellers claimed their help. And here are the jinn, working at full speed for a master who can't see them, fooled by a man leaning on a stick.
The only one who knew was a small creature chewing wood. In the Qur'an, the unseen, al-ghayb, belongs to Allah. Not to jinn, not to kings, not to anyone with a reputation for secret knowledge.
And a second, gentler point. Sulayman, who had armies and wind and jinn at his command, died as everyone dies, here standing up, in the middle of an ordinary day. The verse doesn't mock him.
It just tells the truth about how little anyone knows.

how: Muslims believe knowledge of the unseen (al-ghayb) belongs to Allah alone, and many scholars cite this verse when warning against fortune-telling and claims that jinn reveal hidden things.

games.q: you're one of the jinn, building for Sulayman. he stands over you, leaning on his staff, day after day. what do you do?
games.why: they kept working. only when a creature ate through the staff and he fell did they realize they didn't know the unseen.

practice: Think of one person you'll see today, and quietly list what you don't actually know about them: what they're carrying, what they're afraid of, what happened this morning.
Let the list get long, and notice how much of a day runs on guesses. If you'd like, rest in the verse's idea: what's unseen is held by Someone, not by anyone's guesses.

wordCard.voice: Sulayman, son of Dawud, the king whose staff was gnawed through by a small creature while the jinn kept working, unaware he had died. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a creature of the earth, the small thing that gnawed Sulayman's staff.
